clue.text: Companies hurl insults, finally

parts.note: to hurl something is to cast or throw it

indicators.note: finally asks for only the closing letter of the word insults

explanation.surface: Firms trading abuse, the last word in a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes S, the last letter of 'insults', after CAST. The definition means theatre companies, the groups of actors in plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical company is the troupe of actors in a show, also called its cast.

clue.text: Group's search cut short with German golfer's support

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter of the word for search is lopped off

parts.note: to comb an area is to search it thoroughly
mit is the German word for with
a golfer rests the ball on a tee before driving

explanation.surface: A team hunting briefly for a German golfer's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' takes the last letter off COMB, leaving COM; MIT is German for 'with'. 'German golfer' looks like one person, but 'with German' gives one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A panel of people appointed to handle some business is a body or board.

clue.text: Pet's drink's knocked over

indicators.note: knocked over means tipped upside down, which in a down clue reads the word in reverse

parts.note: port is a fortified wine, and drink's here gives port plus S, a drink is

explanation.surface: Someone's pet has spilt its water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked over' turns PORTS backwards. 'Pet' is not an animal but an old word for a fit of sulking.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet is a fit of bad temper or sulk, as is a strop.

clue.text: Follows and watches programmes, interrupted by advert

indicators.note: interrupted by means broken into, so the advert sits inside the programmes

parts.note: TV programmes are shows
an ad is an advert

explanation.surface: Viewing television shows that keep breaking for adverts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interrupted by' puts AD inside SHOWS.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone secretly and keep an eye on them is to dog their steps.

clue.text: New red coat — Edward's smartened up

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of red coat are made into something fresh, a rearrangement

parts.note: Ed is the short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Edward has had a fresh red coat and looks smarter for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges RED COAT into DECORAT, then ED (short for Edward) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorated room or house has been painted or adorned, made smarter.

clue.text: Rubbish cricket shot with little length

parts.note: a drive is a full-swinging attacking stroke in cricket
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: A poor cricket stroke on a short ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little length' means the short form of 'length', L. 'Length' is also cricket talk for where the ball lands, which fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivel is foolish talk, nonsense.

clue.text: Animal found eating curry on a regular basis

indicators.note: eating means taking inside, so the word for found swallows the chosen letters

parts.note: to found something is to create or establish it

indicators.note: on a regular basis asks for every other letter of the word curry

explanation.surface: A beast discovered chomping curry regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a regular basis' takes U and R from 'curry', and 'eating' puts them inside CREATE. 'found' reads as 'discovered', but it means 'establish'.
explanation.definitionFit: Any living beast or being can be called a creature.

clue.text: Naughty children from class are almost out of order

indicators.note: out of order means not in the proper sequence, so the letters are rearranged
almost means not quite all, so the word are loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Unruly pupils from a class that is misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ARE to AR, and 'out of order' rearranges CLASS plus AR. 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Rascals are mischievous young scamps.

clue.text: Call footballer over, restrained by the short one

indicators.note: restrained by means held in, so the reversed footballer sits within the shortened word
short means the word the loses its final letter
over means turned the other way, so the footballer's name is read backwards

parts.note: Pele was the great Brazilian footballer

explanation.surface: Calling a footballer across, only to have him held back by a short player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns PELE into ELEP, 'short' cuts THE to TH, and 'restrained by' puts ELEP inside TH, with ONE after.
explanation.definitionFit: To call someone is to ring them on the phone.

clue.text: Fear religious education bores papa

indicators.note: bores means drills into, so religious education goes inside the father

parts.note: papa and dad both mean father
RE is the school subject religious education

explanation.surface: Dad dreads the RE lesson because it bores him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bores' looks like 'is tedious to', but it means 'drills into': RE goes inside DAD. RE is Religious Education, a UK school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is great apprehension or terror.

clue.text: Adult possibly angrier after beginning of middle-age spread

indicators.note: after places the anagram behind the letter taken from middle-age
beginning of asks for just the opening letter of the word middle-age

parts.note: A is the film-certificate abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters could be arranged another way, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: An adult who gets crosser once middle-age spread sets in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' shuffles A (adult) plus ANGRIER into ARGARINE; 'after' puts that behind M, the first letter of 'middle-age'. The phrase 'middle-age spread' hides the definition, the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Margarine is a butter substitute, a fat you spread on bread.

clue.text: Student enthralled by free ointment

indicators.note: enthralled by means held captive inside, so the student's letter goes within the other word

parts.note: to free someone from danger is to save or rescue them
L is the learner plate, standing for a student driver

explanation.surface: A student captivated by a free cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enthralled by' puts L (a learner, so a student) inside SAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A salve is a soothing balm or cream put on wounds.

clue.text: Politician restricted by different role, I pray

indicators.note: restricted by means confined within, so the politician sits inside the rearranged letters
different signals that role and I appear in a changed order

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament, a politician

explanation.surface: Someone praying that a politician is kept in a different job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges ROLE and I into I...LORE, and 'restricted by' puts MP inside that. The 'I' belongs to the wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore is to beg or beseech earnestly, much as one prays.

clue.text: Go backwards around piano, getting stuck

indicators.note: around shows the reversed word wraps itself about the musical letter
backwards tells us the word for go is written from right to left

parts.note: to go is to leave or depart
p is the musical marking for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: Reversing round a piano and getting wedged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backwards' turns DEPART into TRAPED, and 'around' wraps that about P (piano).
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught with no way out means being stuck fast.

clue.text: Urge to drink Tango? Husband first removes top

parts.note: Tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: removes top means the leading letter of the word first is dropped

explanation.surface: Fancy a Tango? A husband strips off first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removes top' drops the F from FIRST to leave IRST, after T (Tango) and H (husband). Tango looks like the fizzy drink in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A craving for liquid is the desire felt when the body needs water.

clue.text: In front of team, allude to missing maiden target

indicators.note: front of asks for the opening letter of the word team
missing means lacking, so the letter for maiden is taken out

parts.note: to allude to something is to mention it
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: Hinting at a goal in front of the side, without mentioning a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front of' takes T from 'team', and 'missing' removes M from MENTION, leaving ENTION. 'In front of' reads as one phrase, but IN is a piece. In cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is an aim or goal, what one sets out to do.

clue.text: Dismiss brief encounter on holiday

parts.note: a brush is a fleeting contact, a brief encounter
someone on holiday is off work

explanation.surface: Writing off a short holiday romance.
explanation.walkthrough: BRUSH OFF is used as a verb here, meaning to rebuff someone. Brief Encounter is also the title of a classic British film about a passing romance.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the cold shoulder is to reject them curtly, sending them away.

clue.text: Tease workers appearing in newspaper with small busts

indicators.note: appearing in means shown inside, so the tease and workers go within the newspaper

parts.note: the FT is the Financial Times newspaper
to rag someone is to tease them
men is a common word for workers

explanation.surface: Workers teased in the paper about small sculptures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appearing in' puts RAG and MEN inside FT, then S follows. 'busts' reads as statues, but it is a verb, breaks into pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To shatter something into bits is to break or bust it apart.

clue.text: Cook rice first, not second? Fantastic!

indicators.note: cook can mean falsify or tamper with, so the letters are juggled
not tells us the letter for second is left out of the word first

explanation.surface: Instructions to cook rice first, then a cry of delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not second' drops S from FIRST, giving FIRT, and 'Cook' rearranges RICE plus FIRT.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrific is an exclamation of delight meaning superb.

clue.text: Editor securing new literary composition is named

indicators.note: securing means holding fast inside, so the editor's letters enclose the rest

parts.note: publishers call a book a title, a literary work on their list

explanation.surface: An editor taking on a new book, which gets a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'securing' puts N (new) and TITLE inside ED. Publishers count their books as titles; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A work called by some name is said to bear that heading or label.

clue.text: Drink that is something you might get in a cafe

definitions.text: something you might get in a cafe

parts.note: to drink to someone's health is to toast them
ie is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A drink, and something to eat with it at a cafe.
explanation.walkthrough: A toastie is British slang for a toasted sandwich, a cafe staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A grilled sandwich is a typical snack served in a coffee shop.

clue.text: Cream ordered with a brownie?

definitions.note: the Brownie was a cheap box model made by Kodak

indicators.note: ordered here means put into a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking for cream with a chocolate cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges CREAM and A. The question mark flags that 'brownie' is an example, the Kodak Brownie, not the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kodak Brownie was a popular snapshot device for taking photos.

clue.text: Putting up with a large round racket

indicators.note: round means placed around, so the word for large surrounds the racket

parts.note: big means large
a din is a racket, a loud noise

explanation.surface: Tolerating a huge round of noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts BIG around DIN, after A. 'racket' reads as the sports bat, but it means noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Abiding something means enduring or tolerating it.

clue.text: The man's admitting upper-class brother's arrogance

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the man's word takes the upper-class and brother letters inside

parts.note: his means belonging to the man

explanation.surface: A man conceding that his posh brother is conceited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' puts U (upper-class) and BR (brother) inside HIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Hubris is excessive pride or overweening self-confidence.

clue.text: France — not just a place to go for amusement

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France
something not just is unjust or unfair

explanation.surface: France is more than just somewhere to enjoy yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not just' reads in the surface as 'not only', but it means UNFAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground with rides and stalls is somewhere people visit for fun.

clue.text: Dukes initially seen wearing suits

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so the suits word goes round the first letter

parts.note: something that suits you fits you

indicators.note: initially asks for the first letter of the word seen

explanation.surface: Dukes first seen in suits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes S from 'seen', and 'wearing' puts it inside FITS. 'Dukes' is slang for fists, as in 'put up your dukes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes is old slang for the hands clenched for fighting.

clue.text: Gun no good, I establish? This is given to a new soldier

definitions.text: This is given to a new soldier

indicators.note: no tells us the letter for good is taken away from the word gun

parts.note: to form something is to establish or set it up

explanation.surface: A recruit asking whether a useless gun is what he must set up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' takes G (good) out of GUN, leaving UN, then I and FORM follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Recruits are issued with the standard outfit of their regiment.

clue.text: Socialist party upset stranger

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down clue reads both words backwards

parts.note: a red is a socialist or communist
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A socialist party disturbed by an outsider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns RED and DO together, giving the answer read upwards. 'stranger' looks like a noun, but it means more strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Odder is the comparative of odd, meaning more peculiar.

clue.text: Fleet Street houses with interesting features, primarily

indicators.note: houses means contains, so the abbreviation for street holds the selected letters
primarily asks for the first letter of each of the three words that follow

explanation.surface: Fleet Street, home to buildings of note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' takes W, I and F from 'with interesting features', and 'houses' puts them inside ST. 'Fleet Street' reads as London's old newspaper district, but 'Fleet' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means fast, quick on one's feet.

clue.text: For ex-president, Boxing Day is banned

indicators.note: Boxing here means putting in a box, so the president's name encloses the day's letter

parts.note: Joe Biden is a former US president

explanation.surface: For a former president, Boxing Day is off-limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' puts D (day) inside BIDEN. Boxing Day is the UK holiday on December 26th, here split into indicator and fodder; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something prohibited is not allowed, outlawed.

clue.text: Bird stretches?

parts.note: bird and stretch are both slang for a term spent in prison, so several birds are several such terms

explanation.surface: A bird spreading its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is rhyming slang, bird lime for time, meaning time in jail; a 'stretch' is also a jail term. The plural of both is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Prison terms handed down by a judge are what convicts serve.

clue.text: Young women from opposite directions surrounded by American soldiers

indicators.note: surrounded by means placed within, so the directions go inside the soldiers

parts.note: GIs are US soldiers
right and left, R and L, are opposite directions

explanation.surface: Young women hemmed in by American troops on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded by' puts R and L (right and left) inside GIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Female youngsters are lasses or maidens.
